title: The Teaching Moment of Applying Values to Problems
author: Admired Leadership
summary: When a junior team member brings a leader a problem they cannot solve, the reflex is to supply the answer; this piece argues the better move is to convert the request into instruction in the organisation’s values. The proposed method is specific: point the person to the stated set of values or guiding principles, ask them to work out an initial solution themselves in light of what the team stands for, and withhold the leader’s own application of those values. The pay-off is doubled — the problem gets solved, and the team member discovers that values which had seemed decorative are in fact operational, which retroactively explains why the organisation invested in articulating them. The essay is candid about its precondition: the technique only works where a succinct set of values has already been socialised and genuinely accepted. Where values are empty words and lofty aspirations, there is nothing to apply. The closing argument ties the practice to culture maintenance, since culture is simply the aggregate of values team members express daily, and solutions untied to values are treated as a cultural failure.
points: The specific instructional move is to have the team member pre-load a solution against the team’s stated values before the leader offers any view — withholding the answer is what makes it teaching rather than help.
The technique doubles as a test of the values themselves: if they cannot be applied to a live, gnarly problem, they were aspirational slogans rather than guiding principles.
The author argues that team members only come to appreciate why an organisation laboured over its values once they have used them practically.
Culture is framed as a daily aggregate — what team members express in their choices — so each values-free solution is a small cultural loss rather than a neutral outcome.
quotes: Inexperienced team members or those new to the team often confront gnarly problems where the solution is not obvious, at least to them.
Rather than simply giving them the answer, the best leaders use the opportunity and treat it as an important teaching moment.
Asking the team member to consider the problem in light of what the organization stands for and to apply the values of the team directly to the problem can turn on light bulbs.
Good leaders still resist telling others how to apply these values but instead ask them to do an initial calculus themselves.
When team values are just a set of empty words and lofty aspirations, they can’t easily be applied in any practical way.
Because organizational cultures directly reflect the values team members express daily, this exercise is more important than first meets the eye.
Applying values to address problems is something every leader and team member can and should get better at. Any solutions not tied to values are a miss of cultural proportions.
